tone_statements.quote: Basically there are two discrete tone levels, high and low, together with a feature of downstep, lowering of the high tone level (3.14). Tone signals lexical contrasts … and also has direct semantic relevance in that it realizes features of tense and polarity in the structure of the Verbal Group (3.5) … gliding tones occur only on the final syllable of the word-piece. … Underlying tones on all non-final syllables in the word-piece are simple, being either high or low. Underlying tones on all final syllables are complex, being a combination of two tones

Ch. 2 'The phonological hierarchy' (pp. 33-60: phoneme, syllable-piece, word-piece, phonological phrase = one intonation contour, phonological sentence) and ch. 3 'Tone' (pp. 61-98) describe two discrete tone levels (H, L) plus downstep, lexical and grammatical tone; the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the (good ABBYY) text; no culminative prominence is described at word rank.

tone.quote: Basically there are two discrete tone levels, high and low, together with a feature of downstep, lowering of the high tone level (3.14). Tone signals lexical contrasts … and also has direct semantic relevance in that it realizes features of tense and polarity in the structure of the Verbal Group (3.5) … gliding tones occur only on the final syllable of the word-piece. … Underlying tones on all non-final syllables in the word-piece are simple, being either high or low. Underlying tones on all final syllables are complex, being a combination of two tones
tone.says: Two level tones, high and low, with distinctive (non-automatic) downstep of high, partly from latent low tones; falling/rising glides only word-finally, analysed as HL/LH; tone marks tense/polarity.

sources.note: Part One sect. 2 (p. 3): 'Mbembe also has two contrastive tones, high and low' plus downstep marked with !; no stress statement. Only use of the word is a dialect note, sect. 8(e) p. 20: 'In Osopong dialect, when the sounds o and a come in the middle of a word, they are pronounced in the same way, very short and unstressed.' Part Four (orthography statement) is announced but absent from this conversion.

sources.citation: Pike, Kenneth L. 1966. Tagmemic and matrix linguistics applied to selected African languages. Final report (ERIC ED010547). Ann Arbor: Univ. of Michigan CRLLB, 295 pp. - incl. Barnwell 'Notes on the Mbembe clause system' (App. I) and Revill 'Preliminary report on para-linguistics in Mbembe (E. Nigeria)' (App. VIII, pp. 245-251).
sources.note: Nothing on Mbembe word stress (Barnwell's appendix is clause syntax; Revill's treats emotional intonation/voice quality, noting 'phonemic tone contrasts are preserved'). The statement 'Stress is not phonemic.. the stress is born by the syllable with the highest tone' on p. 281 belongs to the Legbo (Agbo) routine phonological statement, a neighbouring language, not Mbembe.

sources.note: The orthography sheet gives a 'Tone:' block listing two tones, high (acute accent) and low (grave accent), and states that tone is marked only on a few words where ambiguity might arise; no mention of downstep, contour tones or stress. Also notes fortis ('dotted') vowels contrast only in root-nuclear position and vowel length for /a/, /o/ only. PHOIBLE AA 781 encodes this as 2 tonemes (high, low). Thin secondary statement consistent with Barnwell's two-level (+downstep) analysis.
